name: 5480 BC Radiocarbon Excursion (debated)

phenomena.details: Very large ~20 per mil 14C increase over ~10-15 years with a multi-phase profile unlike an impulsive SPE; interpretation debated between an anomalous grand-minimum onset and a cluster of solar proton events.

impacts.description: Sustained elevation of atmospheric radiocarbon production over a decade or more, indicating an unusual and prolonged change in solar activity or particle flux.
Prehistoric anomaly with no written record; known only from tree-ring radiocarbon.

papers.title: Large 14C excursion in 5480 BC indicates an abnormal sun in the mid-Holocene
papers.authors: Miyake, F., Jull, A. J. T., Panyushkina, I. P., et al.
papers.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.keyFinding: Found a ~20 per mil 14C increase whose prolonged, multi-phase shape cannot be explained by a single solar proton event, suggesting an unusual grand-minimum onset, a series of SPEs, or a combination.

summary: A very large but unusually shaped radiocarbon excursion centred on the 5480s BC. The signal is real and well measured, but its cause is debated and it is not a clean single solar particle event.
description: Miyake et al. (2017) measured a ~20 per mil increase in tree-ring radiocarbon over roughly a decade beginning around 5481 BC - larger in total amplitude than the AD 774/775 event. However, its time signature is anomalous: instead of the sharp 1-2 year rise and decay expected from an impulsive solar proton event, it shows a rapid rise followed by a prolonged, plateau-like enhancement lasting around fifteen years. The inferred production rate approaches the theoretical zero-modulation maximum, which strains a pure grand-solar-minimum explanation, while the long duration strains a single-SPE explanation. The authors propose it reflects an unusual state of a grand solar minimum, a cluster of successive solar proton events, or a combination of the two. It is included here as a debated case rather than a confirmed single extreme SPE.
